blocks.text: Long before anyone wrote them down, Turkmen folk tales, *ertekiler* (one tale is an *erteki*), were told aloud and passed from one generation to the next. Folklorists usually sort them into three kinds: tales about animals, magic tales full of wonders, and tales of everyday life.

Almost every tale opens the same way: *Bir bar eken, bir ýok eken*, literally **there was one, there wasn't one**, the Turkmen **once upon a time**. The formula is so familiar that it has served as the title of tale collections, from a book of 37 tales published in 1937 to one sold in the country's bookshops today.

Listen to the verbs and you can hear the teller's distance from the story. The scene is set with *eken*, and the action moves on in `-(Y)pdYr`, the two ways of this unit for telling what the speaker didn't see: *Bir obada bir garry adam bar eken…* (In a village there was an old man…) *Bir gün ol bazara gidipdir* (One day he went to the market).

The heroes are mostly ordinary people rather than princes. Surveys of Turkmen literature name characters from the common people, such as Aldar Köse, Kelje and Dälije, who come out on top in hard situations through hard work, skill, quick wits and courage. Aldar Köse, the beardless trickster, is known all over Central Asia; among Turkmens, though, the short comic stories more often belong to Ependi, the wise fool you met in [A1 unit 4](a1-u04-culture).

The tales reached print in the early 20th century. From 1914 to 1917 an Ashgabat newspaper published them under the heading *Erteki*. In 1926 and 1927 the folklorist Alişbek Aliýew (1883–1933) brought out *Türkmen ertekileri* (Turkmen tales) in two parts, with stories such as *Akylly daýhan* (The clever farmer), *Möjek hem tilki* (The wolf and the fox) and *Üç ogry* (Three thieves). Bigger collections followed: *Türkmen halk ertekileri* (Turkmen folk tales) in 1940, a three-volume edition in 1978–1980, and a book of fifty tales from the Academy of Sciences in 1986.

Tellers close a tale with a rhyme, too. One recorded among the Turkmens of Iran is *Myrat myradyna ýetdi*: **the one who longed got his wish**, a play on the name *Myrat*, which means **wish**. New collections are sold in the country's bookshops today, and the Dovletmammet Azadi National Institute of World Languages in Ashgabat has had many tales translated, into languages from English and Russian to Korean and Arabic.

blocks.title: Reading a tale
blocks.text: You can follow the start of most tales with three things: *Bir bar eken, bir ýok eken*; *bar eken* for **there was**; and verbs in `-(Y)pdYr` for what happened next: *görüpdir* (saw), *gidipdir* (went), *aýdypdyr* (said).
With the words of this unit, you can read the start of a tale:

blocks.tk: Bir bar eken, bir ýok eken, bir çölde bir tilki bar eken. Tilki örän akylly eken. Bir gün ol bir möjegi görüpdir. Möjek uly we aç eken. Tilki gaçypdyr.
blocks.en: Once upon a time, in a desert, there was a fox. The fox was very clever. One day it saw a wolf. The wolf was big and hungry. The fox ran away.

vocab.tk: Bir bar eken, bir ýok eken
vocab.en: once upon a time (literally: there was one, there wasn't one)

questions.q: In a tale, what does *Bir bar eken, bir ýok eken* mean?
questions.explain: **One day** is *bir gün*, which comes later in the tale.

questions.q: Why are the actions in a tale told with `-(Y)pdYr`?
options: The teller didn't see them happen
questions.explain: `-(Y)pdYr` tells what the speaker knows from others, as a storyteller does.

questions.q: In the reading, what does the fox do at the end?
